disease_info: Bipolar II disorder is characterized by a recurrent course of major depressive episodes and hypomanic episodes, without any history of a full manic episode. Depressive phases tend to be prominent and impairing, often driving help‑seeking, while hypomanic periods may be experienced as productive or ego‑syntonic and therefore underreported. Onset is typically in adolescence or early adulthood, but many patients present later in life after years of fluctuating mood and energy that were never formally diagnosed. It is distinguished from unipolar depression by the presence of at least one hypomanic episode and from bipolar I disorder by the absence of mania and generally less severe mood elevation, though functional and psychosocial impact over time can still be substantial.

narrative.stressor: In the year leading up to presentation, Miguel had been shortlisted for a regional director role, which meant longer hours at the distribution center, more travel, and pressure to deliver cost savings while managing a wave of turnover among his supervisors. He initially rode a surge of energy and ideas, taking on extra projects, volunteering for late shifts, and spending more nights in the garage tinkering with his motorcycle and woodworking instead of resting. Over several months, the “high gear” periods at work began to alternate with stretches when he struggled to keep up with planning meetings and performance reviews, falling behind on reports and skipping his usual church fellowship and fishing weekends. When a trusted younger colleague quietly told him that his leadership had become unpredictable—swinging from overzealous initiative to disengaged absence—Miguel agreed to see his primary doctor, who, noting a longstanding pattern of mood and energy shifts rather than a simple work burnout, referred him to psychiatry.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I just can’t think straight or make decisions at work the way I used to.”

narrative.stressor: As Julissa and her husband began seriously discussing her gradual retirement from community association management, she agreed to cut her hours and hand off several long‑standing properties to a younger colleague. What she expected to be a graceful easing into more time for hiking, cultural festivals, and family gatherings instead left her feeling unmoored, with stretches of overcommitting to new volunteer and sustainability projects followed by periods where she withdrew from her book club and left household tasks unfinished. Her family noticed that in the months after reducing her workload, her mood and drive seemed to swing more sharply than the stress she described, and she became increasingly preoccupied with whether she had "wasted" her life and career despite others’ reassurance. When she confided to her daughter during a Smoky Mountains planning session that she had been dwelling on death and questioning whether her family would be better off without her, her daughter brought her to an urgent primary care visit, which led to an expedited psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve been thinking about death a lot and wondering if my family would be better off without me.”

narrative.stressor: Don’s mood and energy shifts became more noticeable after he moved in with his girlfriend and ramped up his role leading municipal park design teams, juggling early‑morning site work, evening community meetings, and weekend art and hiking plans. At first, his girlfriend appreciated his bursts of enthusiasm—taking on extra design work, reorganizing the apartment, and planning elaborate road trips—but grew frustrated when these phases were followed by weeks where he cancelled social plans, lost interest in shared hobbies, and let bills and house projects slide. Their arguments about his inconsistency and her concerns that he might be "losing interest" in the relationship prompted him to look back and realize that similar cycles had strained past relationships and community commitments as well. When she suggested couples counseling, the intake clinician, hearing about longstanding patterns of alternating high‑energy project sprees and periods of disengagement, recommended an individual psychiatric evaluation instead, which Don agreed to after noticing he could no longer stay engaged in the landscaping and art projects that normally excited him.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep losing interest in the projects and activities I usually care about, even when everything in my life is going fine.”
